proposed_claims.statement: Openings-rate mean was 1.6042 percentage points higher in 2022-2024 among months with unemployment 3.5-4.5%
2024-only gap was smaller than pooled post-2021 gap
Conditional comparison does not establish a structural or causal shift
The pilot reproduces a known descriptive gap that narrowed by 2024 and cannot claim novelty or causality

works.title: Job openings and the Beveridge curve, December 2000–April 2013
The Shifting Reasons for Beveridge-Curve Shifts
What Caused the Beveridge Curve to Shift Higher in the United States During the Pandemic?

comparisons.prior_claim: The agency documented the same aggregate unemployment–openings relationship in an earlier period.
comparisons.source_excerpt: The Beveridge curve is a graphical representation of the relationship between the unemployment rate and the job openings rate.
comparisons.difference: BLS plots the same aggregate relation only through April 2013, so it cannot contain the pilot’s later numerical comparison.

comparisons.prior_claim: The working paper surveys shifts and their changing drivers through 2023.
comparisons.source_excerpt: Figure 1: U.S. Beveridge curve: December 2000 - August 2023.
comparisons.difference: NBER already displays the pandemic separation through August 2023; the exact frozen band mean and 2024 endpoint are later arithmetic.

comparisons.prior_claim: The IMF paper studies the pandemic shift with state data and a search model.
comparisons.source_excerpt: The Beveridge curve in the United States has shifted substantially higher since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic
comparisons.difference: IMF establishes the outward pandemic pattern, but its vacancy measure uses vacancies divided by labor force, so its plotted magnitude is not numerically interchangeable with the pilot’s JOLTS openings rate.

comparisons.prior_claim: The agency documented the same aggregate unemployment–openings relationship in an earlier period.
comparisons.source_excerpt: From 2010 to the present, the point moved up and to the left as the job openings rate increased and the unemployment rate decreased.
comparisons.difference: This older movement gives no evidence about 2024; the pilot updates the endpoint, while using an established display.

comparisons.prior_claim: The working paper surveys shifts and their changing drivers through 2023.
comparisons.source_excerpt: Since the summer of 2022, the empirical Beveridge curve has exhibited what looks like a puzzling, vertical drop.
comparisons.difference: NBER documents falling vacancies with little unemployment increase before 2024; the pilot’s 2024-only mean is a later update.

comparisons.prior_claim: The IMF paper studies the pandemic shift with state data and a search model.
comparisons.source_excerpt: Many of the factors mentioned here will fade in importance as time goes on, suggesting that a progressive partial renormalization of the Beveridge curve could take place.
comparisons.difference: IMF anticipates possible partial reversal; it does not observe the pilot’s 2024-only arithmetic.

comparisons.prior_claim: The agency documented the same aggregate unemployment–openings relationship in an earlier period.
comparisons.source_excerpt: The outward shift in the Beveridge curve may be due to a greater mismatch between available jobs and the unemployed in terms of skills or location, or that employers are delaying hiring due to economic uncertainty.
comparisons.difference: BLS itself offers competing explanations; the pilot likewise cannot identify a cause from the aggregate chart.

comparisons.prior_claim: The working paper surveys shifts and their changing drivers through 2023.
comparisons.source_excerpt: the reasons for why the Beveridge curve shifts, and how and whether they also affect job creation, cannot be gleaned from movements in the unemployment and job openings rates alone.
comparisons.difference: The same nonidentification warning applies directly to the pilot’s two-rate comparison.

comparisons.prior_claim: The IMF paper studies the pandemic shift with state data and a search model.
comparisons.source_excerpt: The reduced form specification is liable to the critique that it may incorrectly identify vertical shifts in the curve that actually capture horizontal shifts of a steeply sloped curve
comparisons.difference: Even the richer IMF specification flags a shift-identification problem; the pilot’s band means are less informative.

comparisons.prior_claim: The agency documented the same aggregate unemployment–openings relationship in an earlier period.
comparisons.source_excerpt: From 2010 to the present, the point moved up and to the left as the job openings rate increased and the unemployment rate decreased.
comparisons.difference: BLS establishes the descriptive method and historical movement, but its 2013 endpoint cannot show a 2024 narrowing.

comparisons.prior_claim: The working paper surveys shifts and their changing drivers through 2023.
comparisons.source_excerpt: Since the summer of 2022, the empirical Beveridge curve has exhibited what looks like a puzzling, vertical drop.
comparisons.difference: The prior paper already addresses the subsequent decline; the pilot extends the endpoint through 2024 without a new mechanism.

comparisons.prior_claim: The IMF paper studies the pandemic shift with state data and a search model.
comparisons.source_excerpt: Many of the factors mentioned here will fade in importance as time goes on, suggesting that a progressive partial renormalization of the Beveridge curve could take place.
comparisons.difference: Prior work offers mechanisms and predicts possible reversal; the pilot adds a 2024 descriptive endpoint only.

independent_review.rationale: I independently checked all 12 claim-by-work excerpts at their retained HTML or physical PDF-page pointers, read the surrounding passages, matched all three full-text hashes, and checked publication dates against the BLS, NBER, and IMF publisher records. The revised matrix correctly separates BLS's pre-pandemic descriptive evidence, NBER's observed 2022-23 decline, and IMF's forecast of possible partial renormalization from the pilot's 2024-only arithmetic; it also notes the IMF vacancy denominator difference. The October 2023 NBER date is appropriately month-precise. The 2024 endpoint adds a bounded descriptive replication update, not a new mechanism, causal result, or top-journal contribution. This attestation approves the honest replicate decision and source tracing only; it does not certify novelty or manuscript acceptance.
